iberia.description:
Iberia’s Migration polity is the Visigothic Kingdom after Vandal/Alan passage—Arian then Catholic, Toledo-centred, harshening toward Jews, genetically Hispano-Roman with limited Gothic input relative to political power. Reccared’s 589 conversion and the Liber Iudiciorum push unity of Goth and Roman under faith and code. Isidore of Seville organises encyclopaedic Christian knowledge for a post-Roman West.

Gothic language fades; Romance and Latin win—a classic elite dominance without permanent language replacement. Votive crowns at Guarrazar and compact churches visualise royal piety. The kingdom Islam will shatter in 711 still bequeaths law, councils, and Isidore’s filing cabinet to medieval Europe.

Spain’s Migration face is Catholic monarchy forged from foederati origins—gold for altars, councils for orthodoxy, encyclopedia for clerks.

Clerical computus, not laboratories, structures learned time. Technical knowledge serving Visigothic Hispania is practical before it is theoretical: farming calendars, craft recipes, fortification, navigation, computus, and the accounting of tribute or estate. Measurement, memory, and logistics are the sciences that keep polities alive between harvests and wars.
iberia.philosophy: Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies organise Christian encyclopaedism—language, nature, sacred history—for a post-Roman West. Conciliar Toledo defines orthodoxy as royal-philosophical duty. Formal schools are scarce or clerical; worldview is nonetheless coherent in rite, counsel, and moral tale. For Visigothic Hispania, right conduct is taught through custom, confession, and memorable example rather than through a university curriculum—named thinkers appear only where the record truly preserves them.

britain.description:
Britain’s Migration polity is a split island: Anglo-Saxon settlement and kingdom-making in east and south, Brittonic kingdoms holding west and north. Archaeology shows new burial rites; genetics argue substantial but variable North Sea influx. Christianity survives in the west; pagan English convert around the turn of the seventh century. Sutton Hoo and inscribed western stones answer each other across a cultural frontier.

Adventus myths, heptarchy kingship, and missions from Rome and Iona remake lowland Britain as English-speaking Christian realms while Brittonic speech and saints’ cults persist. Law codes begin to turn conquest into order; heroic poetry and penitentials teach rival ethics of fame and humility.

The polity click must hold both stories: ship burial gold and Atlantic crosses—making and survival.

france.description:
Gaul’s Migration polity is Clovis’s Franks conquering rival kingdoms and choosing Catholic baptism, aligning with Gallo-Roman bishops. Merovingian rule overlays Roman cities and law with warrior kingship. Ancestry mixes late Roman Gallic populations with northern Frankish input—political transformation with demographic layers, not Beaker-scale replacement. The ethnonym will become France while speech trends Romance.

Childeric’s Tournai treasure and Merovingian garnet cloisonné set warrior bling against saint cults and baptisteries. Salic custom and royal retinues rebuild Gaul as a Christian kingdom claiming Roman inheritance without restoring the empire. Gregory of Tours will later moralise the dynasty’s crimes and miracles as divine commentary.

France’s Migration panel is baptismal conquest: the font as founding constitution.

central.description:
On the map’s Polish polity click, Migration-Period Poland is dominated by the Wielbark archaeological horizon—Gothic-linked in standard narratives—centred on Pomerania and the Vistula corridor. Cemeteries favour bi-ritual burial, often weaponless, with paired fibulae and amber; settlements fade mid-fifth century as the landscape empties or transforms before early Slavic horizons. Portable dress, not stone capitals, carries style and status.

Political ideas survive as practice: costume codes, cemetery continuity, and eventual south-east mobility rather than a written Polish state ideology. Amber–Roman exchange along the Vistula organises prestige while kinship groups negotiate climate, neighbours, and opportunity. Later Slavic incomers bring different household rites into the same riverscape, beginning a new demographic chapter atop Migration-era absences.

Poland’s Migration panel is therefore archaeology’s detective story: graves hinting at peoples later famous on the Black Sea and in Italy, without yet a Piast chronicle to name them.

italy.description:
Italy’s Migration polity is Odovacer then Theodoric’s Ostrogothic rule over a still-Roman peninsula, followed by Justinian’s devastating Gothic War and the Lombard entry of 568 in the north. Ravenna paints Arian and court mosaics onto late Roman brick; Boethius and Cassiodorus keep philosophy and administration literate under Gothic kings. Ancestry remains late antique Italian continua under successive military elites; Gothic language is temporary, Romance and Latin continuity prevail.

The political experiment of civilitas—Goths as army, Romans as civil society—advertises restoration while hiding fragility. When Eastern imperial armies come to ‘liberate,’ Italy learns that reconquest can cost more than barbarian peace. Lombard duchies then fragment the north into a new early medieval map.

Italy’s panel is the Migration Age’s most Roman tragedy: mosaics of order, prisons of philosophy, and war that unmakes both.

balkans.description: Eastern Rome holds Constantinople and fights Goths, Huns, Avars, and Slavic settlement. Balkan provinces transform demographically with Slavicization uneven by valley. Genetics: late Roman + Slavic-associated mobility — debated proportions, real cultural change.

eastern.description:
Ukraine’s Migration click centres on the Chernyakhov multiethnic horizon with Gothic elites on the forest-steppe, later shocked by Hunnic mobility. Open villages yield wheel-made grey wares, glass cups, bone combs, and Wielbark-style fibulae; aesthetic power sits in ceramic standardisation and dress sets, not cities. Hunnic-period gold later overlays the same corridors.

Ideas of kingship—Ermanaric in legend—float above mixed Sarmatian, Germanic, and local farming populations sharing one material package. Conversion-era Gothic Christianity belongs to the wider Gothic story; customary law and sacral kingship are remembered in Getica more than in local treatises. When Hunnic pressure rises, westward Gothic movements remake European politics from this Pontic doorstep.

The polity panel is mixture under hierarchy: a grey-ware civilisation facing Rome and the steppe at once.

ITA.science: Aqueducts, surveying, medical handbooks, and mosaic workshops keep late antique technology alive. Ravenna’s engineers and copyists preserve more than they invent until Justinian’s wars disrupt the system. Technical knowledge serving Ostrogothic & late antique Italy is practical before it is theoretical: farming calendars, craft recipes, fortification, navigation, computus, and the accounting of tribute or estate. Measurement, memory, and logistics are the sciences that keep polities alive between harvests and wars.
ITA.philosophy: Boethius’ Consolation fuses Neoplatonism and prison ethics at Theodoric’s court; Arian–Nicene tension is the public metaphysics. Philosophy is still Greek-Latin school inheritance, now under Gothic kings. Formal schools are scarce or clerical; worldview is nonetheless coherent in rite, counsel, and moral tale. For Ostrogothic & late antique Italy, right conduct is taught through custom, confession, and memorable example rather than through a university curriculum—named thinkers appear only where the record truly preserves them.
ITA.art: Ostrogothic Ravenna—Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, Arian Baptistery, Theodoric’s mausoleum—keeps Italy a mosaic-and-marble civilisation under Gothic military dress. Art insists on imperial memory even when emperors no longer live in the West.
ITA.ideas: Theodoric’s civilitas: Goths as army, Romans as civil society, Amal kingship under Eastern imperial grant. Cassiodorus’ letters advertise continuity of Roman administration after 476’s symbolic end. Political imagination under Ostrogothic & late antique Italy turns on legitimacy—who may command, tax, baptise, or bury with honour—and on the stories that make conquest or continuity feel rightful. Ideas circulate in law, sermon, treaty, and rumour long before they harden into institutions.
ITA.literature: Cassiodorus and Boethius try to keep Latin thought alive under Gothic kings; the Consolation of Philosophy is a prison lamp. Ostrogothic Ravenna speaks in mosaic as much as in edict.

ESP.description:
Iberia’s Migration polity is the Visigothic Kingdom after Vandal/Alan passage—Arian then Catholic, Toledo-centred, harshening toward Jews, genetically Hispano-Roman with limited Gothic input relative to political power. Reccared’s 589 conversion and the Liber Iudiciorum push unity of Goth and Roman under faith and code. Isidore of Seville organises encyclopaedic Christian knowledge for a post-Roman West.

Gothic language fades; Romance and Latin win—a classic elite dominance without permanent language replacement. Votive crowns at Guarrazar and compact churches visualise royal piety. The kingdom Islam will shatter in 711 still bequeaths law, councils, and Isidore’s filing cabinet to medieval Europe.

Spain’s Migration face is Catholic monarchy forged from foederati origins—gold for altars, councils for orthodoxy, encyclopedia for clerks.

FRA.description:
Gaul’s Migration polity is Clovis’s Franks conquering rival kingdoms and choosing Catholic baptism, aligning with Gallo-Roman bishops. Merovingian rule overlays Roman cities and law with warrior kingship. Ancestry mixes late Roman Gallic populations with northern Frankish input—political transformation with demographic layers, not Beaker-scale replacement. The ethnonym will become France while speech trends Romance.

Childeric’s Tournai treasure and Merovingian garnet cloisonné set warrior bling against saint cults and baptisteries. Salic custom and royal retinues rebuild Gaul as a Christian kingdom claiming Roman inheritance without restoring the empire. Gregory of Tours will later moralise the dynasty’s crimes and miracles as divine commentary.

France’s Migration panel is baptismal conquest: the font as founding constitution.

GBR.description:
Britain’s Migration polity is a split island: Anglo-Saxon settlement and kingdom-making in east and south, Brittonic kingdoms holding west and north. Archaeology shows new burial rites; genetics argue substantial but variable North Sea influx. Christianity survives in the west; pagan English convert around the turn of the seventh century. Sutton Hoo and inscribed western stones answer each other across a cultural frontier.

Adventus myths, heptarchy kingship, and missions from Rome and Iona remake lowland Britain as English-speaking Christian realms while Brittonic speech and saints’ cults persist. Law codes begin to turn conquest into order; heroic poetry and penitentials teach rival ethics of fame and humility.

The polity click must hold both stories: ship burial gold and Atlantic crosses—making and survival.

HUN.description:
Hungary’s Migration click is the Hunnic-period Carpathian Basin—imperial confederation prestige kit of polychrome cloisonné, horse gear, and cauldrons worn by many peoples. Attila’s tribute diplomacy and multiethnic vassalage organise the middle Danube until 453. Ideas of empire here are charismatic and extractive compared with Rome’s paperwork; monumental stone is scarce.

Roman writers cast the Hun as scourge; inside the confederation, ideology is loyalty to the king and redistribution of plunder. Composite bows and cavalry logistics are applied sciences; isotopes now track mobility. After Attila, subject peoples fracture the system—Gepids and others inherit pieces of a short hegemony.

The basin’s panel is gold, horses, and sudden kingship that remakes Europe without founding a long archive.

TUR.description:
The Turkish/Anatolian polity click in Migration time is Eastern Roman Constantinople radiating law, orthodoxy, and early Byzantine aesthetics toward a fracturing West. Ivories, silks, and church programmes define imperial Christian taste; Neoplatonism and Chalcedonian Christology dominate elite metaphysics. Foederati policy and Persian/Danube frontiers structure strategy.

While Gothic and Frankish kingdoms experiment in the West, New Rome claims universal order with Greek schools, medical handbooks, and fortification science. Administrative numeracy is survival technology amid demographic shocks. The capital’s idea of itself—Roman continuity—becomes the Migration Age’s longest successful political theology.

Turkey’s panel is the empire that did not fall when the West did—already Byzantine in soul.

DEU.description:
Germany’s Migration polity covers Alamannic and early Frankish row-grave zones east of the Rhine—weapons, brooches, belt fittings, Roman spolia reuse—without a single capital’s mosaic programme. Confederate Alamanni and expanding Franks renegotiate the old limes world; political ideas are pagi, war-bands, and gradual Merovingian overlordship rather than a German nation.

Pagan sacral landscapes yield piecemeal to Frankish-sponsored Christianisation. Honour, feud, and local cult structure right conduct before cathedral schools. Iron weapon production, upland clearance, and Rhine crossing knowledge are frontier sciences; Roman fort stone becomes quarry and mnemonic.

DEU’s panel is frontier ethnogenesis: the middle Rhine as workshop of peoples who will later fill Carolingian East Francia.
